item.title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvgyyw2jeego?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal - Published Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping within seven days because "they're losing so badly". In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response. He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past. Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June. Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week. The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February. "I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers. Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently". He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them." Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful. He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government". Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?" He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face. Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks. Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis. Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway. Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker. Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage". "President Trump's right to reject it," he said. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the US were taking a toll on Iran. Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran. The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners. These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran. Related topics - Published4 days ago

item.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5ywnp075d1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead - Published Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country. Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured. In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks. In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing. Police said thirteen men and four women were killed. Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African. He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups. Mining without permission in abandoned shafts or dump sites is a persistent problem in South Africa, causing numerous deaths from unsafe conditions. Authorities say the miners are typically undocumented migrants recruited by organised crime gangs. Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP. He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects. In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital. No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning. The two mass shootings came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township. Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million. But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining. In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development". Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence. On Saturday, a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni, to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths.

item.title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckpq0g7z5pjjo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections - Published Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption. Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade. He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution. The pro-Russian populist's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting. It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof, killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024. Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed. Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress. A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality. Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation. This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year. Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands. He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics. Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected. Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS. The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia. Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade, becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017. He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment. item.title: Two bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan climbing group
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwjdvml9e897o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan climbing group - Published Rescuers have recovered two bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas. Around a dozen people are still thought to be missing after a sheet of snow fell on the base camp of Himlung Himal peak on Manang district on Sunday morning. The group of Nepalese nationals, including climbers and support staff, had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp and fix ropes on the mountain. Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet. Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams initially unable to reach the site. Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP that at least eight members of his expedition team had been reported missing. The exact number of climbers still unaccounted for remains unclear. A rescue team consisting of experienced mountaineers was rushed from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, via helicopter. That effort is now expected to continue on Monday due to the thick snow and bad weather, local media report. The Nepalese team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain. Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry. Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches. The latest death of Nepalese climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja. It also comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August. More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements. Extreme weather events have also affected other parts of Asia in the past week. Extreme weather in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said. Meanwhile, a flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok because of heavy rainfall since Thursday, with people being urged to stay at home or move to higher floors. Earlier this week, a deadly typhoon that battered Tokyo, triggering landslides in neighbouring prefectures that killed four people. Typhoon Dujuan was the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", an area of warmer sea water that facilitates the formation of powerful storms. item.title: Four killed in helicopter crash near Montreal
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3grvv7p81lqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four killed in helicopter crash near Montreal - Published Four people have died after a helicopter crashed in a small town 50km (31 miles) from Montreal, Quebec's provincial police have told the BBC. Emergency services were called to Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville shortly after 14:30 local time (18:30 GMT) on Saturday afternoon, where they found the aircraft on fire and declared its occupants dead at the scene. The victims have not yet been identified but the aircraft appeared to be a private helicopter, Sgt Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said. An investigation into the crash is being led by the Major Crime Unit of the Sûreté du Québec, working alongside crime scene technicians as well as investigators from the Transportation Safety Board of Canada. The crash site is located near the Rang des Écossais road off Highway 10, according to Bilodeau. Police were notified of a helicopter in distress that may have crashed and caught fire in an emergency call. An hour after the call, the fire at the site had been brought under control, though officials were still working at the crash site just before 22:00 local time. The victims have not yet been identified and Bilodeau said this process may "take a few days." Related topics - Published2 days ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1wxxzn5jndo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey - Published Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events. The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine. In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree. The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware. A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday. NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines. "Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater." In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead. Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather. Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said. item.title: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c620lrw2xr12o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow - Published Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York. Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro. Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday. Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure. However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end". Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president. Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres. Foro Penal confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo Cedeño, who it said had been arbitrarily detained since June 2019. Also released was Frank Cabañas, who rights groups say had been held in prison for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Foro Penal said he was the only suspect who remained detained, despite family members reporting that he was suffering health problems last year. Opposition and human rights groups have said Maduro's government used the detention of political prisoners to stamp out dissent and silence critics for years. Rodriguez has sought to frame her interim government as more permissive of political dissent while currying favour with the US. The prisoner release scheme was a key concession by her administration to the US. However, her decision to end the scheme attracted criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said it was stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released. Rodriguez's government continues to deny dissidents are jailed. It has cast the release of prisoners as a gesture of goodwill and reconciliation. Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace". But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls – that the US has previously endorsed – for swift elections. Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight." Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote. Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader María Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January. Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held. Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when. item.title: Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y5nj8ejj8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes - Published Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance". The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France. A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years. The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse. The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context. "It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance." The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters. Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy. The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement. "It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added. The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak. Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile. On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron. During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed". The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church". "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said. The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000. But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025. Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s. The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK. Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world. A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys. Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church, and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse, but problems remain. Later on Sunday, the Pope met staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, and took part in a torchlight procession. It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025. Popes have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots. - Published1 day ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim too
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pwl9g9ne1lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim too - Published Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee. Pike told Sellars she did not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says. Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when Colleen was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men. Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting". But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, while UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider. "It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence. "Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness." In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later, it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened. But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged over a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge. In 2021, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since. Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her. "Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says. Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation." Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable." 'She should pay for it' Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution. A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy. Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021. Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment and Lee has never before granted clemency in a death penalty case. The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps. On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it. Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution. "She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments. Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did." "My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added. "There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting." The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution. The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it was what Colleen's family want. "We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed." Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption. "When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says. "These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else." Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime. "People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says. "Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live." item.title: Woman charged with stealing from patients and staff at hospitals across Ontario
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3ew9e5lg01vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Woman charged with stealing from patients and staff at hospitals across Ontario - Published Police in Ontario, Canada, have charged a woman with 65 offences including fraud and theft for allegedly stealing from patients and staff at several healthcare centres in the province. Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) identified the suspect as Nassim Eronn, 34, from Burlington, a city 56km (34 miles) south of Toronto. "The investigation was initiated following multiple reports of theft and fraud involving patients and staff members within healthcare facilities," police said in a statement to BBC News. They say the incidents under investigation began in February 2024 and continued until as recently as last month. The suspect worked at health centres across the province. The suspect faces charges including 34 counts of fraud under $5,000 (£3,800), 13 counts of theft under $5,000 and seven counts of disobeying a court order, according to police. Other charges include breach of trust and impersonation. OPP began investigating the woman in May after a report of theft when she worked at Orillia Soldiers' Memorial Hospital, about 130km north of Toronto. "This investigation was prompted by several complaints of theft and fraud from patients and staff within the hospital," police said at the time. The investigation was expanded to cover more hospitals where further incidents were uncovered. "Multiple search warrants were executed where significant amounts of property were seized," police said. It is unclear what were the suspect's specific duties at the hospitals. item.title: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm750plvwy9vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality - Published Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality. More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed. The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment. Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties. Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia. "People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility". While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference". He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace". Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe. This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv. Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees. Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s. Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

item.title: German town bans 'stumbling stone' memorials to Nazi victims
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm2mm4y5dkko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
German town bans 'stumbling stone' memorials to Nazi victims - Published There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis. Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal". Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities. The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations. But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones in their town. The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects. The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate. Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated. However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision. "Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild. She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision. Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach". She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD". Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance. In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings. As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location. Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen". The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects. Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. item.title: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
item.description:

Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged - Published Warning: This story contains distressing details The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene. Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August. The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree. "I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC. The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged". Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging. Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black. "I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way. "Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?" Fortune's death left the local community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion. Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought. "When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people." When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down". Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs. Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction. "Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said. "If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does." She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes. Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.

Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared - Published A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after more than 300mm (12in) of rain fell since Thursday, leaving roads in the Thai capital submerged. On Sunday, Bangkok's Metropolitan Authority said the rains have subsided, but canal water levels remain high. The city's governor has warned that the flooding is not yet over. People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors. Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested. Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now. "I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now." She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding. Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding. The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand. All 50 of Bangkok's districts were declared emergency zones. On Saturday, Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported. He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled." Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published3 days ago

British national among six dead in building explosion close to Acropolis in Athens - Published Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens. The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis. Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building. Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast. The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police. item.title: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq4g55r76d9lo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says - Published An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year. The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA. It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers. The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025. Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed. University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says. "But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds. Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note. They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team. A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said. The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures. However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety. Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action. The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones. "The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day." When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement. The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events. UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations". It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures that are common practice at US high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors. Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead. His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Related topics - Published10 September

item.title: Brazil's Lula bans online gambling ahead of presidential election
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c914ddj21rzlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Brazil's Lula bans online gambling ahead of presidential election - Published Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has announced a ban on online gambling, just days before an election in which he is seeking a fourth term as the country's leader. The left-wing leader, who is running against the son of the incarcerated former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, signed a provisional order on Friday that "prohibits all sports betting and online casinos". The online gambling industry in Brazil was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction. Flávio Bolsonaro accused his rival of playing politics, while Brazilian football teams said the ban could lose them income due to betting firms pulling their sponsorships. Lula described the industry as a "cancer" in his announcement, adding that "either we remove the tumour, or it kills us". The move comes just over a week before the first round of Brazil's presidential election. Recent polls have the 80-year-old leader almost neck-and-neck with the younger Bolsonaro. Lula also separately signed a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common type of online sports betting. Punters and bookies will have until 5 October to withdraw any existing funds from online betting accounts, while new deposits have been barred. The new measures must receive congressional approval within 120 days to remain in force. Lula acknowledged online betting was allowed under the former President Michel Temer's administration but said that it had grown "without regulation under Bolsonaro's management". He said in a statement on X that there were "no restrictions" particularly for preventing children and teenagers from accessing online betting. "We won't allow betting companies to profit at the expense of Brazilian families' income and lives," the president added. Lula described how he had heard from families who had sold everything in their houses because of their gambling addictions. Earlier this week at the UN General Assembly, Lula accused the industry of "transforming addiction into profit". But Flávio Bolsonaro called the gambling crackdown "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday, according to Reuters. Grêmio, one of the so-called "big twelve" Brazilian football teams, noted ahead of Lula's announcement that sports betting firms had become "one of the main sources of revenue for sports" since they were made legal. It said a change in the law "will not only be an open door for illegal betting, but a fatal blow to Brazilian football, leading many clubs to insolvency". The main clubs were paid 1.1bn Brazilian reais ($212m; £160m) by sports betting firms in 2025, while the industry took in 62.5bn reais at the same time, broadcaster Globo reports. Most types of gambling, such as casinos and slot machines, are illegal in Brazil, but ever since online betting was legalised in 2018, it has exploded in popularity. About 59.9% of Brazilian adults support banning internet betting, a survey by Atlas and Bloomberg published this week has found. The Brazilian Institute for Responsible Gaming (IBJR), a trade body representing around 75% of the domestic betting sector, said a total ban on fixed-odds betting jeopardised the industry as a whole – and potentially 58-73bn real in revenue. "The ban also doesn't eliminate existing demand," it said in a statement, adding that anyone turning to illicit betting would no longer have "access to protection mechanisms provided in the regulated environment". It urged the federal government to strengthen betting regulations rather than outlaw online and fixed-odds betting entirely. Related topics - Published18 August - Published13 August

item.title: Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq39me84zrkdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Before BTS and Blackpink, there was Big Bang: Now the Kings of K-pop are back - Published A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean. An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back. Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour. Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history. As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming. For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia. Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia. The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal. Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking. Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community. By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging. The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful. In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards. When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours. They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible. Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List. "When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool. "Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds. "Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be." Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies. But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre. For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live. "They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore. "They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me." The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS. And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong. In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks. But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise. "Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology." The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow. Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years. Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances. Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success. South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus. Then came the scandals. In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group. Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal. It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars. South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement. Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience. Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more. "Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs." The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong. The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition. Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted. While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances. Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets. "I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy." For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance. "I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin. "Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream." Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube. "Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um. "It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations." While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life. As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd. Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut. As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop. item.title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq70dgdndr46o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety - Published "A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol". Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation. And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it. China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up. "The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home. "People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me." She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting". Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media. In Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better. These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times". "Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore. "But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it." He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia. Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it. China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development". Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air. "The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected. This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful." Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us." Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things." Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation. Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money." And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says. Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them. They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job. Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals. Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward. Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition. The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home. "When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution." About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles". Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation. But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity. "If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."
